blocks.text: …me,” he said, tapping the photograph. “I was nine years old. And your father pulled me out of a collapsed trench with his bare hands.”

His name was Richard Hale. In 1986, his father owned a small construction company in Fort Worth. My dad was a twenty-three-year-old laborer. One Saturday, Richard tagged along to a job site and wandered into a drainage trench. The wall gave way. My father jumped in without waiting for anyone and dug him out before the dirt covered his face.

“My father never forgot it,” Richard said. “Two years later, the company nearly went bankrupt. Your dad had a little savings, money he’d been putting away for a house. He lent it to my father, no contract, just a handshake. It kept us alive. When my father tried to pay it back with interest, yours refused the interest. He said, ‘Just make sure Richie grows up to be the kind of man who helps somebody else.'”

Richard grew up and took over. Today his company builds hospitals and schools across Texas. And through a holding company, he owns a stake in several businesses around Dallas, including the dealership that had just fired me.

“Your father called me four months ago,” he said. “He knew he was sick. He didn’t ask me for anything. He just said he was proud of you, and that he hoped someday I’d look in on you. I was flying in for the funeral when I stopped by the dealership to introduce myself. Your manager told me you’d been fired ‘for choosing a funeral over your job.’ I asked whose funeral. He didn’t know. He didn’t care.”

That was the meeting with the owner. My manager wasn’t fired for firing me; he was fired because when the owner pulled his file, there were eleven other complaints from employees denied bereavement leave, sick leave, even a day for a child’s surgery.

Richard opened the box again. Under the photograph was a check made out to my father, dated 1988, for the full amount of that loan plus thirty-eight years of interest. My father had never cashed it. He’d kept it in a drawer, Richard said, as a reminder that some debts are better as friendships.
“It’s yours now,” Richard said. “And so is a job offer, if you want it.”

I didn’t go back to the dealership. I went to work for Richard’s company as a project coordinator. The dealership did call, though. The owner wanted me to know they’d rewritten their leave policy. Five paid days of bereavement for every employee, effective immediately.
I cashed the check and paid off my mother’s mortgage. On the memo line of the deposit slip, I wrote: “For the house you were saving for, Dad.”
